signals.title: Alibaba Unveils Qwen4-Max: New AI Teammate for Work, Creativity, and Discovery - Alibaba Cloud
signals.excerpt:
Hangzhou, China, November 16, 2026 - Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, the most capable model in the Qwen family to date. Featuring 2.4 trillion total parameters, native vision capabilities, and a one-million-token context window, Qwen4-Max excels at complex tasks across work, creativity, and research. Qwen4-Max achieves top rankings across leading benchmarks, particularly in coding, agentic tasks and visual reasoning. It ranked 6th on Code Arena, a real-world coding leaderboard, and posted strong scores across specialized benchmarks for agent workflows, workplace productivity, and visual reasoning, including Agents' Last Exam, Vals Index, JobBench, and Chartography. According to Work360—a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields—Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%. These gains are driven by the new Qwen4 architecture, which upgrades the sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design across attention, residual connections, and embeddings. Built as an MoE model with 2.4 trillion total parameters, Qwen4-Max activates only 71 billion per token—25% fewer activated parameters compared to Qwen3.8-Max at the same 2.4T scale—delivering stronger capabilities at a lower inference cost. Qwen4-Max is available now on QwenCloud via the Token Plan and API. Users can also access the model across Alibaba platforms, including QwenWork and QwenStudio. Input (Implicit Cache Hit) is priced at $0.075 per 1M tokens. Open-weight, smaller-scale models from the Qwen4 series will soon be released to developers worldwide.

...

Qwen4-Max features advanced Cloud Resource Scheduling capabilities designed for deployment in cloud infrastructure. Operating in a closed loop, the model autonomously optimizes its own scheduling workflows to cut costs and boost resource efficiency. In benchmark testing, this reduced data-annotation model call costs by an average of 9%, and accelerated offline CPU rescheduling speeds by more than 14 times. Beyond cloud infrastructure, Qwen4-Max supports professional workflow and creative production such as 3D modeling, game development, and agentic video creation. In automotive manufacturing, Qwen4-Max delivers end-to-end capabilities across production-line planning, part design, and machining verification. During a showcase, the model cut manual workpiece programming time by 95%—from roughly 475 minutes to just 24 minutes—by using feedback-driven iteration to catch overcuts and insufficient material removal before machining begins. Qwen4-Max also accelerates forward-deployed engineering (FDE) across industries such as finance, law, healthcare.

signals.title: Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU
signals.excerpt:
Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.

The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.

LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.

...

## A sample deployment runs on 194 Huawei chips

Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.

This version is available in a separate repository. The self-hosting guide describes a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend accelerators from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.

signals.title: Neo4j releases Relate, an open source in-memory database built for AI agents
signals.excerpt:
## The short version

- Relate is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and built in Rust
- It runs in-process, in memory, with optional disk storage for durability
- It includes an MCP server, a command-line tool, and Bolt and HTTP query endpoints
- Errors carry retryable flags, and a row cap stops large results from flooding an agent
- Neo4j cites Gartner: machine users reach 75% of database workloads by 2029

...

Neo4j, a company that makes graph databases, has released Relate. A graph database stores information as things and the connections between them, which suits questions like "who is linked to whom, and through what." As Cyprus Shipping News reported, Relate is open source, written in the Rust programming language, and aimed at AI agents and the systems built around them.

...

Connectivity comes built in. Relate has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a common standard for letting agents use outside tools, plus a command-line tool. It also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints, so existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks and developer tools should work with it.

## Graph queries and retrieval

Relate supports Cypher, the query language Neo4j uses for graph data. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity, which finds items with similar meaning, and follow connections through the graph in the same step. Neo4j says this supports multi-hop reasoning, where an answer depends on following several links in a row, and GraphRAG, which feeds a model facts drawn from a graph. The company says this gives agents more accurate results and fewer hallucinations, meaning invented answers. That claim is Neo4j's and is not tested in the source.

The release says Relate is 100% openCypher compliant and more than 97% compliant with GQL, the standard graph query language. Those numbers suggest queries written for other graph systems may carry over, though the source does not say how that was measured. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, a permissive open source license.

signals.title: New Research Challenges GPU Utilization as Measure of Inference Infrastructure
signals.excerpt:
New NAND Research report underscores that busy GPUs aren't an accurate measure of productive output; introduces new Inference Economics Scorecard to measure inference infrastructure by the useful work it delivers, as applied in an eight-hour benchmark with Nebius on NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs and WEKA NeuralMesh.

CHICAGO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- From Supercomputing 2026: WEKA, the AI data and memory infrastructure company, in collaboration with market intelligence firm NAND Research, today introduced the Inference Economics Scorecard, a new common framework for measuring inference infrastructure productivity and economic value by the useful work it delivers rather than by how busy it keeps GPUs. The scorecard defines nine measures, including tokens per watt, cost per inference, and context retention. It sets four testing rules, including runs of at least eight hours and counting only successful output. Already applied in a benchmark with Nebius, the AI cloud company, it comes as inference is claiming a growing share of AI infrastructure spending and buyers hit power, memory, and rack-space limits.

...

For years, training was the dominant AI workload. Because training keeps GPUs busy with large, predictable jobs, GPU utilization became the default measure of AI infrastructure productivity. Inference, especially agentic inference, places very different demands on GPUs. An agent does not simply answer a prompt; it completes a task over many steps, and at each step it re-reads the context it built earlier. After the GPU evicts that context from memory to make room for other users and sessions, it must recompute it when the task returns, and the task makes no further progress until that work is done. The result is a GPU that is fully utilized but unproductive because it wastes cycles recomputing the same tokens multiple times.

The Inference Economics Scorecard measures inference systems at production scale: completed requests across many concurrent users, sustained over hours rather than minutes.

...

From Busy to Productive: How the Scorecard Works The Inference Economics Scorecard defines nine measures of inference performance and economics: tokens per watt, tokens per rack, cost per inference, GPU goodput, time to first token and end-to-end latency, memory efficiency, operational density, agent concurrency, and context retention. It also sets the discipline for testing against them:

- The same workload and service targets across every system tested
- Measurement of the whole serving stack
- Runs of at least eight hours
- Only successful output counted

...

Putting It to the Test: Real Agent Load, Sustained for Eight Hours WEKA and Nebius recently applied the scorecard's rules in a joint benchmark on NVIDIA HGX B300 systems and reported results on several measures. The test ran on one eight-GPU node serving DeepSeek-V4-Pro to 512 active sessions drawn from a corpus of more than 5,000 real agentic coding sessions over eight hours per configuration, counting every failed and timed-out request.

Using WEKA NeuralMesh with Augmented Memory Grid, which pools NVMe across the cluster as a shared context tier, the node produced 3.7x the output tokens per GPU-hour compared with HBM-only serving on the same GPUs, and 97% of successfully completed requests reached a first token within five seconds, up from 44%. On HBM-only serving, 60% of prefill work was recomputed from context the cluster had already processed earlier in the session; with Augmented Memory Grid, 6.8%. At the measured rate, the HBM-only node would need about 30 hours to produce what Augmented Memory Grid produced in eight. The full benchmark is published at weka.io and nebius.com blogs.

Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
## Park idle agent sessions in object storage

Agent Substrate and AX are built for that: the developer's session stays open, and the sandbox that serves it gives its machine back while the session waits. Together they cover the parts of an agentic platform that are the same for every team: the control plane, the runtime, and the sandbox. Agent Substrate answers where and how an agent runs. AX answers what the agent is.

Following the CNCF donation of gVisor, Agent Substrate, and OpenRL in November 2026, you have the flexibility to run this open source, agentic platform across any environment. Agent Substrate 1.0 is generally available on GKE.

...

Agent Substrate answers where and how an agent runs. It separates the stateful agent from the compute it runs on. An actor is the sandbox for one agent, and it holds the agent's running processes, files, and identity. A worker is a reusable sandbox drawn from a warm pool of Kubernetes Pods, and one worker hosts several actors.

An agent runs code that a model wrote, so anything in its environment can leak through a prompt injection or a bad command, API keys included. Gateways control the actor's inbound and outbound traffic and add credentials on the way out, based on the actor's identity, so the agent never holds the keys.

signals.title: Huawei open-sources MACaQ quantization tool for model compression · Wortins
signals.excerpt:
# Huawei open-sources MACaQ quantization tool for model compression

The story

Huawei has released MACaQ, an open-source tool that squeezes large language models down to a fraction of their size without the usual multi-machine setup. The company says it can compress a 122-billion-parameter model to 4-bit precision in about 64 minutes on a single GPU, a job that normally demands far more hardware and time.

Quantization, the process of storing a model's weights at lower precision, is how big models get small enough to run on modest machines. Doing it fast, on one GPU, lowers the barrier for researchers and smaller companies that cannot afford sprawling clusters, and it fits Huawei's broader push to build an AI stack that does not depend on restricted Western chips.

signals.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient - Microsoft Research
signals.excerpt:
## At a glance

- Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches.
- TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model.
- Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable.

...

In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents, we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on.

...

After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it.

Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use, while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed.

Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself.

...

TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation.

...

The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know.

- Model-specific GPU execution optimizations such as DeepSeek's MegaMoE kernel and Qwen's multi-token prediction with Tensor Core verification reduce data movement and sequential decoding steps.

MLPerf Endpoints v1.0 evaluates this balance between serving capacity and responsiveness using coding and enterprise workflows through API endpoints. During performance runs, generated tool calls and workflow intent are checked against reference values. Separate SWE-bench Verified evaluations assess end-to-end task-solving capability. In MLPerf Endpoints v1.0, provisional NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 results show over 10x the throughput per kilowatt of provisioned power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at a shared minimum end-to-end interactivity of 50 tokens per second per user. 1 

This post presents the benchmark results and outlines the hardware and software optimizations used in the submissions.

...

| Model | Throughput per provisioned kW ratio | E2E interactivity ratio |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kimi K3 | 10x | 3x |
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash | 9x | 5x |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 5x | 3x |

...

## Hardware and software optimizations for agentic inference

NVIDIA Rubin GPUs combine HBM4 memory, NVIDIA Tensor Cores, and sixth-generation NVIDIA NVLink to support the demands of agentic inference. HBM4 enables rapid access to model weights and conversation state, Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations, and NVLink supports communication across GPUs. Context-aware serving and model-specific kernels build on these capabilities to reuse prior work, independently optimize prefill and decode, and accelerate token generation—translating hardware advances into greater inference capacity and faster interactions.

### Context-aware serving and model-specific optimizations improve inference performance

Agentic workloads repeatedly reuse conversation history while adding new instructions and tool results. Efficient serving must preserve reusable state, distribute requests across workers, and accommodate the different execution requirements of prompt processing and token generation. Prefix caching, state reuse, and NVIDIA Dynamo routing help reduce redundant computation and balance serving load, while disaggregated serving supports independent optimization of prefill and decode.

...

| Optimization | How it improves performance |
| --- | --- |
| Context reuse and routing | Reuse previously processed conversation state and distribute requests to reduce recomputation and balance worker load. Example: Qwen’s fine-grained prefix matching reuses previously processed history across turns. |
| Prefill and decode optimization | Configure prompt processing and token generation independently through disaggregated serving, reducing contention and synchronization waits. Example: Kimi combines disaggregated serving with prefill changes that reduce GPU synchronization waits. |
| Model-specific GPU execution | Tailor kernels, fusion, and memory access to each architecture, reducing kernel launches and data movement. Example: DeepSeek’s MegaMoE kernel uses Rubin GPU locality and matrix-multiply instructions. |
| Speculative generation and verification | Propose multiple tokens and verify them together, reducing sequential decoding steps. Example: Qwen’s multi-token prediction pairs token proposals with Tensor Core verification. |

signals.title:
Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

...

The contract is simple: across sampler decode, serving prefill, and trainer forward, all three paths must produce bitwise-identical logprobs for every sampled action—comparing raw floating-point bytes under the same rollout weights, token history, and sampling settings, with zero rounding or tolerance.

...

Our work delivers an open-source, modular JAX/XLA and Pallas implementation of this contract for TPU in Tunix. Verified across a multi-host 64 TPU v5p (DP8×TP8) mesh, these kernel and collective patterns provide a reusable blueprint that teams can adopt to achieve bit-exact on-policy RL across distributed JAX/TPU stacks.

...

To benchmark our TPU kernels, we run a 200-step numerical verification test on the synthetic FrozenLake environment using a public Qwen3-8B checkpoint as a baseline test case using 64 TPU v5p chips with a DP8×TP8 mesh. The recipe uses a GSPO-token loss with leave-one-out advantages. We compare Standard training with trainer-old logprobs and no additional sampler correction, token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS), and Zero-TIM.

...

Zero-TIM records zero mean absolute sampler–trainer logprob difference at every logged step in this window, while its training solve rate increases. Standard and TIS retain nonzero differences: TIS adjusts their contribution to the update without removing the underlying mismatch. Zero-TIM reaches higher observed solve rates in these runs.

signals.title: RAG's Trust Problem: Citations, Memory, and Benchmarks Don't Add Up Quite Right - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
This digest covers RAG/GraphRAG developments from 2026-11-09 through 2026-11-16: a dense week on arXiv and Hugging Face Daily Papers, a seven-post knowledge-layer push from Neo4j, and one methodology post each from LangChain and LlamaIndex.

## 🔥 Highlights 

1. A 45-Minute Answer to One Question — graph-grounded context turns hours of log-diving into one query.
2. Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation — up to 15.7% of RAG citations don't actually trace to retrieval.
3. MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System — new state of the art on LoCoMo and LongMemEval agent-memory benchmarks.
4. Introducing ParseBench-2 — a severity-weighted benchmark exposes where document parsers break RAG upstream. 
5. DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory — argues agent memory's real bottleneck is writing, not retrieving.

...

- RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG — 2026-11-13 — Jointly optimizes discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding parameters for the query-rewriting stage of RAG instead of tuning them separately and statically. Query rewriting is usually the brittle, hand-tuned piece of production RAG pipelines, so a joint optimization approach is directly applicable to teams fighting noisy retrieval feedback on complex queries.
- Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution — 2026-11-12 — Introduces MAPE, which evolves whole memory-management programs (not just hyperparameters) via an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop, gaining up to 12% absolute accuracy over hand-designed baselines on LoCoMo/LongMemEval at a third of the serving cost. Suggests automating memory-architecture search rather than hand-crafting write/read/consolidation policies.
- RMIT-ADM+S at TREC RAG 2026: Research Agents, Retriever Ablations, and Open-Weight Replication — 2026-11-12 — A TREC 2026 RAG track system paper where six of seven submitted runs beat the track median; writer-model choice and adjacent-chunk expansion turned out to be bigger quality levers than retriever choice alone. Useful competitive-benchmark evidence on where to actually spend engineering effort in a RAG pipeline.
- AutoOntic: Automatic Ontology Induction from Text for Knowledge Graph Construction — 2026-11-11 — Fixes a core GraphRAG weakness: schema-free LLM extraction produces flat graphs with no type hierarchy or domain/range constraints. AutoOntic canonicalizes types and relations and mines hierarchy/constraints automatically — a usable post-processing stage to upgrade flat extracted graphs before GraphRAG retrieval.
- Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-12 — Uses counterfactual substitution (swap a retrieved fact for a false variant and re-query) to measure how often RAG citations actually trace to parametric memory rather than retrieved context: 1.2%–15.7% of citable claims across model families. A hard number on a faithfulness problem that citation-format checks alone won't catch.
- HiddenPathQA: A Benchmark for Knowledge Graph Question Answering When Questions Hide Their Paths — 2026-11-09 — Shows most KGQA benchmarks leak the gold reasoning path in the question's surface tokens, unlike real multi-hop questions that compress chains into a phrase naming no relation. Important for honestly evaluating GraphRAG/KGQA systems — strong scores on existing benchmarks may just reflect surface pattern-matching.
- DISCERN: Preserve at Write, Resolve at Read for Persistent LLM-Agent Memory — 2026-11-11 — Challenges the "memory is just a retrieval problem" assumption: on their ENT-310 benchmark, a vanilla RAG reader already matches strong memory systems on recall since retention/currency are near-saturated. Argues the real bottleneck is write-time contradiction/entity-collision handling — a useful reframing for teams assuming better retrieval alone fixes memory.
- MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents — 2026-11-11 — Notes that the memories most semantically relevant to an agent's state aren't necessarily those that most improve its next action, proposing selection by estimated decision utility instead of embedding-similarity relevance. A concrete, actionable idea: rank agent memory by downstream action impact, not query-memory similarity.
- OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation — 2026-11-10 — Argues RAG's context-length bottleneck is a modality problem, not an information-density one: rendering a document page as an image and using a vision encoder preserves far more detail per token than text compression. A concrete compression-fidelity tradeoff alternative to summarization for teams hitting context-window costs.
- Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation — 2026-11-09 — Shows an agent can match a reference answer even when its visible memory history doesn't actually determine it (a lucky guess), and designs a controlled protocol with byte-identical contexts but different correct answers to detect this. A methodological warning: matching the reference answer is not proof memory was sufficient or used correctly.
- MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System — 2026-11-09 — A multi-agent memory architecture reporting 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, +14.3 points over the strongest baseline, leading on 4 of 5 QA memory benchmarks. Also surfaced on Hugging Face's Nov 16 Daily Papers listing. A strong reference point for benchmarking agent-memory accuracy/cost tradeoffs.
- Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs — 2026-11-11 — An engineering study of multimodal RAG on consumer GPUs (e.g., Tesla T4), quantifying VRAM tradeoffs between quantized weights and co-located vector indices/KV caches. Directly useful for self-hosting RAG on cheaper hardware instead of cloud GPUs.

...

Meanwhile Neo4j's seven-post push and papers like AutoOntic make the opposite-but-complementary case: when you replace embedding similarity with an explicit, queryable graph — an ontology, a decision-precedent graph, a service-dependency graph — you get deterministic, auditable retrieval instead of a probabilistic guess. The week's message for anyone running RAG or GraphRAG in production: measure faithfulness and provenance

signals.title: NVIDIA devblog: GLM-5.3 hits 607.8 tok/s on two DGX Stations | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
## TL;DR

- Two NVIDIA DGX Stations linked by ConnectX-8 RDMA served Z.ai's 753B-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model from one endpoint via vLLM tensor parallelism.
- Throughput peaked at 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16, with time-to-first-token of 482.90 ms, before falling off at higher concurrency.
- The ~464 GB checkpoint was split across two GB300 GPUs (252 GB HBM3e each), using FP8 KV-cache, prefix caching and four-token speculative decoding.

A workable recipe for keeping a frontier-weight Chinese open model entirely on-prem across two workstations is a quiet nudge to enterprises weighing local inference against hosted API dependence.

Two NVIDIA DGX Stations, linked over ConnectX-8 RDMA, served Z.ai's 753-billion-parameter GLM-5.3 model from one endpoint and peaked at 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16, according to a developer blog posted November 13 by Fatima Fall.

The checkpoint runs to about 464 GB, which is more than any single GB300 can hold. "Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine," Fall writes. The vLLM configuration splits the weights across the two GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=2), each holding roughly 218 GiB of weights in 252 GB of HBM3e, and layers on FP8 KV-cache, prefix caching and four-token speculative decoding with a max model length of 98,304 tokens.

The throughput curve is not monotone. At concurrency 32 output falls to 385.0 tok/s and mean request latency climbs to 453.5 seconds, versus 136.46 s at the C16 peak. Fall's framing is dry: "You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory."

signals.title: I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Ok, I made a thing! LLMs have their... quirks. Namely re-reading the same notes, wandering back and forth, and spending 10x more tokens than needed because I can't be explicit.

So I built Haystack — a semantic router for a markdown vault. Instead of the agent digging through files, it queries: hybrid retrieval (embeddings + corpus-IDF term stats, RRF-fused, cross-encoder reranking via llama.cpp), all local, zero cloud, one 35 MB model, ~10 ms per query. MIT, one-command setup: github.com/diogocccarvalho/haystack.

...

Your corrections become regression tests. Every retrieval miss you fix becomes a permanent rule AND a QA pair. The audit reindexes and runs every pair — it exits 1 on a regression, so the same question can't silently fail twice.

And the learned rules only pin when they actually beat retrieval: a stored phrasing must outrank the corpus' own best hit for the same query. Scale-free, not absolute-threshold — so swapping embedders doesn't break your corrections. I A/B'd models against frozen QA sets and rejected two (a reranker that was 2x faster but -16pp Recall@3; a 97M embedder at -7pp). Numbers in docs/RESEARCH.md.

...

## Try it 

```
./setup.sh --start          # model + config + embeddings server, one command
python3 haystack.py reindex
python3 haystack.py query "that thing about the invoices"

```

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works instead (Ollama, LM Studio, remote API). Python 3.11+, stdlib + numpy only — no framework, no vector DB daemon, no cloud.

signals.title: Edge0 Releases 145B and 120B Sparse MoE Models for Single-GPU SSD Streaming
signals.excerpt:
# Edge0 Releases 145B and 120B Sparse MoE Models for Single-GPU SSD Streaming

Edge0 released Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, open-weight sparse MoE models that run on single 24GB GPUs via SSD streaming and native 4-bit NVFP4 quantization.

...

On November 13, 2026, open-source AI developer Edge0 released Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, two open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models engineered to run frontier-level agentic and coding workflows on a single 24GB consumer workstation GPU. By dynamically streaming expert weights from NVMe solid-state storage, the release enables academic laboratories and universities to run hundred-billion-parameter systems locally without incurring recurring cloud API expenses or exposing confidential institutional data off-premises.

...

The Edge0 project announced the public release of its two flagship open-weight models, Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, hosted on the Edge0 Hugging Face repository in native 4-bit NVFP4 and Q3_K formats alongside source code on the Edge0 GitHub repository. Derived from the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next architecture, both models are specialized for autonomous software engineering, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. Unlike conventional dense architectures requiring every parameter to reside in video memory, Edge0 implements a latent sparse MoE structure where only a tiny fraction of parameters activates per token.

The accompanying Edge0 inference runtime (edge0-infer and edge0-strata) establishes a tiered memory architecture. The GPU VRAM stores core attention layers and hot experts, while dormant experts reside in host system RAM and PCIe NVMe storage. Using predictive expert prefetching and zero-copy direct memory access (DMA), the runtime streams weights into VRAM on demand, enabling a 145-billion-parameter foundation model to run on a single desktop GPU like the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090.

...

Deploying a 145-billion-parameter large language model in traditional 16-bit precision requires roughly 290 gigabytes of VRAM—demanding an eight-GPU data center node. Even post-training 4-bit quantization requires 75 to 80 gigabytes of resident memory, far exceeding standard desktop configurations.

Edge0 addresses this constraint through native 4-bit NVFP4 training rather than post-training quantization, preserving mathematical and syntactic precision. Edge0-145B contains 48 transformer layers with 512 sparse experts per layer. The gating router activates 10 routed experts and 1 shared expert per token, yielding approximately 10.12 billion active parameters. Both models support a 256K-token context window using an int8 key-value cache, with 32K tokens retained directly in VRAM. Architectural details published on Edge0’s official documentation portal are detailed below:

...

Hardware throughput figures published by Edge0 and confirmed in technical reviews by eesel AI show that the streaming engine achieves interactive token speeds on consumer hardware. Running on a single RTX 5090 D with 24GB VRAM and a PCIe Gen 4 NVMe drive, Edge0-145B achieved peak agent decode speeds of 98.3 tokens per second, sustaining 80 to 90 tokens per second across multi-turn programming sessions. Prefill throughput reached 3,165 tokens per second at 16K context lengths.

The 120B variant demonstrated even greater throughput: prefill speeds reached 2,668 tokens per second at 4K and 4,357 tokens per second at 16K under NVFP4, while chat decoding averaged 124.9 to 130.2 tokens per second. Agent decode loops reached 135.5 to 144.6 tokens per second. On evaluation benchmarks, Edge0-145B recorded 86.5 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (measuring autonomous CLI tool execution) and 64.6 percent on DeepSWE 1.1 (resolving real GitHub repository pull requests). These figures place the open-weight release alongside proprietary commercial systems while running fully within local workstation limits as open-source software.

...

Edge0 announced that it is preparing pull requests to merge its streaming kernels directly into upstream community engines, including llama.cpp, vLLM, and Ollama, during late November and December 2026. Merging the strata streaming logic into mainstream frameworks will allow researchers to run Edge0 models through standard CLI flags without custom compilation.

signals.title: OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
signals.excerpt:
# OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face

Sasha Blumenfeld · 11/16/2026

We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond. Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face. Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.

The integration also runs the other way. OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them. The setup guide has the steps.

...

Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider. OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability. You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.

You also get automatic failover. If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers. If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.

When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request. Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.

You stay in control of the trade-off. Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as `:fastest`, `:cheapest`, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API. A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.

...

160 models from 38 labs are available this way today, which is every model OpenRouter serves that has a page on the Hub. They include the open-weight models developers use most on OpenRouter, where open-weight models now carry about 70% of paid tokens:

- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
- MoonshotAI Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3
- Z.ai GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash
- Qwen3.8 27B
- MiniMax M3.1 Flash
- Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Flash
- NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra
- OpenAI gpt-oss-120b

...

Add Hugging Face Storage Buckets as a Broadcast destination (it’s in beta) and OpenRouter sends each request as a JSON file to a bucket you own. Each file holds the input messages, the model’s output, token counts, and cost. Images and other media are left out.

...

On Hugging Face:

1. Create a token at hf.co/settings/tokens with the “Make calls to Inference Providers” permission.
2. Open any supported model’s page on the Hub. Chat with it there, or click View code for setup steps for your code or your coding agent, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes Agent.
3. To choose which providers can serve your requests, go to Inference Providers in your Hugging Face settings.
